# Applications for Baylor Applied Performance

## Where this applies

- Inference: Data streams for athletes who do not play on Saturday. A panelist says at least 25 players each week get no game data and calls that an opportunity zone [11:41], and describes using practice tracking over several years to back a player with a small game sample [43:14]. Baylor's GPS and force plate data from practice and testing is the equivalent stream for reserves and redshirts.
- Inference: A minimum-exposure rule per metric before reporting a trait. Kassam says about 60 pass rush snaps could give a get-off number, while a receiver's change of direction might need 200 routes [41:09], [41:41]. These are his vendor metrics, not Baylor's, but the idea of setting a count per metric applies to early-season Catapult and VALD reports.
- Inference: Measurement burden audit. Barwin's account of an HRV check, a hydration check and a survey adding up to too much friction [03:34] is a prompt to list every daily measure an athlete is asked to do and ask which ones change a decision.
- Inference: Position-specific trait definitions in recruiting grading. Caserio says to start from what the player will be asked to do and keep the measurement simple [21:22], and calls most combine drills not real-world applicable [15:47].
- Inference: Communicating findings. Barwin's point that coaches and players want a few items with conviction, not a long cut-up [39:38], suggests a coach report capped at a handful of plays or metrics.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys were abandoned after about a year because athletes learned to game them, and daily countermovement jump mRSI replaced them as the objective readiness marker. The talk agrees about friction and mixed usefulness of daily measures [03:34], and extends the point to player attitude (earlier suspicion, now more conversational) [04:35].
- Eric's baseline: NordBord roster-wide testing was dropped because collection could not be sustained across a large roster; keep demanding tests only with a clear purpose and dedicated oversight. The talk's advice to keep measurement simple and specific [21:22] agrees.
- Eric's baseline (course team position, speaker unconfirmed): weekly tracking is preferred to infrequent testing so plateaus or declines are caught early. The talk's small-sample discussion [40:39] agrees that early data needs care and adds a way to handle it, blending with history [41:41].
- Eric's baseline (course team position): reject "my athletes" ownership language; collaboration across departments is a department operating principle. The talk's emphasis on an integrated building [12:43] agrees.
- Eric's baseline (course team position): a trained coach's eye matters as much as technology. The talk is consistent, with tape plus test numbers as a composite [16:48].

## What would have to be true

- Practice tracking worn consistently, with several seasons of history per player, as Barwin's example required [43:14].
- Agreement among coaches, medicine and performance staff on which few metrics to show.
- Player explanation and buy-in, which Caserio frames as education and a conversation [04:35].
- For a count-based rule, enough Baylor data to see where each metric stabilizes. The talk's numbers come from a different model and dataset.

## Do not apply when

- NFL structure is assumed. Caserio notes football plays few games and practice matters differently [44:14]. College schedules, roster size and practice volume differ.
- A one-team anecdote is treated as evidence. The Eagles practice-tracking example is one case.
- Kassam's snap and route counts are copied as thresholds. They describe his own get-off and COD metrics.
- Barwin's HRV and survey story is used to dismiss all daily monitoring. He says tools have gotten a lot better since.

## First step

List the players who had no Saturday snaps last season and write down which practice or testing data exist for each. Do not change any collection; just see the gaps.

=== FILE: videos/2025-03-18_RZNLXU2O0WM_minding-the-college-football-analytics-gap/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: RZNLXU2O0WM
title: "SSAC25: Minding the College Football Analytics Gap"
event: SSAC25 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Kim Kasam (caption spelling), vice president of product at Teamworks; introduced by Ryan smard (caption spelling)]
topics: [american-football, competitive-advantage, decision-making]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

The speaker, a former first analytics hire at the Pittsburgh Steelers who now works for Teamworks Intelligence, argues that college football analytics sits about a decade behind the NFL and that the gap is about to close. He says free agency, a salary cap and the transfer portal leave small scouting staffs with too many players to evaluate. He describes two tracking-data models his company built: change of direction (COD) and run-game credit attribution. Both are checked against film. He presents a per-game "digital scouting report" for every FBS player as a way to narrow large candidate pools. The claims come from the vendor selling the product.

## Key claims

- College football analytics is about a decade behind the NFL, and the speaker says that gap will close [00:31].
- College evaluation is limited: in-person looks are few, and even big programs may have only three or four scouting staff, with most coaches also scouting [01:31].
- Free agency, a salary cap and the transfer portal now require a few scouts and a position coach to evaluate hundreds of players and make offers within hours [02:01].
- Analytics moved from box scores, to play-by-play data, to ball and player tracking data released to all NFL teams in 2018, and each step needs more people and computing [03:32], [04:02].
- Teams get competitive advantage from the richest data and from doing the most with it, which now means tracking data and a team of people [04:02].
- Straight-line speed alone is not enough; COD matters at every position but is hard to quantify because direction data is noisy [05:34], [06:06].
- COD is measured as a deficit: the same distance run with a turn versus in a line [06:06].
- A COD is found by tracking heading angle over a play and detecting where the turn starts, ends and peaks [07:37].
- Two COD events with a similar deficit can differ in quality, so the model adds entry speed, acceleration, turn angle, rate of turn and distance as context [08:08], [08:38].
- For one 2023 draftee (name garbled in captions), combine 40 and three-cone looked weak while the tracking-based speed and COD looked strong; he was a fifth-round pick [09:39], [10:09], [10:39].
- The speaker treats an "eye test" of a leaderboard as the most important validation; outliers are who teams sign, retain and draft, so mistakes are costly [11:40].
- COD is one piece of the picture and the speaker does not suggest drafting or signing from a COD list [12:10].
- Run-game credit is split into identifying actions and attributing them among 22 players, using a graph neural network with players as nodes and relationships as edges [12:41], [13:11], [14:12], [14:43].
- On one Lions at Chiefs run, the model's expected yardage rises and falls during the play as blocks and defenders act, and credit is given to the runner, blockers and defenders [15:13], [15:44], [16:15].
- The model rewards a defender who runs a long way and penalizes loafing, without being taught this; the speaker says it learned it from about 100,000 running plays [17:16], [17:46].
- Each metric took 4 to 24 months of data science and engineering; the resulting report covers every FBS player and updates after every game [19:52].
- Trait language (change of direction, burst, run blocking) is easier for staff to share than statistics like EPA per play or yards per route run [20:22].
- Teams could use the report to reduce roughly a thousand portal receivers to 20 or 30 [20:52].

## Numbers and definitions

- Decade gap between college and NFL analytics [00:31].
- Three or four scouting department members at a large SEC school [01:31].
- NFL released tracking data to teams in 2018 [03:32]. Another talk in this batch gives 2019.
- More than 70 technical staff, 25 PhDs, a dozen who led R&D departments [04:34].
- COD deficit: time with a turn compared with straight-line time over the same distance [06:36]. The 505 test is described as 15 yards one way, a 180 degree turn, five yards back (as captioned) [06:36].
- Jefferson example: two COD events with a deficit of about a second; one described as an 80 degree dig (as captioned), one a 170 degree hitch [08:08].
- Draftee: fifth round, pick 177 overall [10:09].
- Gibbs play: 18 yards on the play; expected gain about three yards at the start, about eight at its peak; percentile ratings of 96 (acceleration) and 99 (a block) [13:42], [15:13], [15:44], [16:45].
- Mike Dana (caption spelling) ran about 40 yards on the play [17:16].
- About 100,000 running plays seen by the model [17:46].
- "Two dozen models" sometimes calibrated together [18:50].
- 4 to 24 months per metric [19:52].
- Portal opens April 16th; a thousand receivers to 20 or 30 [20:52].
- Quote of 10 or 15 plays a season as the margin; the speaker thinks it underestimates [21:55].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Research first, then build on published sport-science ideas (COD deficit) [06:06].
- Signal detection on the heading angle curve (gradient to find start, end and apex of a turn) [07:37].
- Context adjustment for COD expectations [08:38].
- Graph neural network for action identification and attribution in the run game [14:12].
- Validation by a leaderboard "eye test" and by returning to film [11:09], [11:40].
- Metrics built from ball and player tracking data [09:09].

## Limits and open questions

- No validation statistics, error rates or hit rates are shown; the main evidence is single-player examples and a leaderboard eye test.
- The Nacua and Gibbs examples are chosen cases; no sample of misses is shown.
- Metric definitions, model inputs and COD noise handling are described only at a high level.
- The speaker says a COD list should not be used alone [12:10].
- Commercial source: the talk presents the speaker's own company's product.
- The speaker says high school data is not available [22:58], so the approach reaches only players with all-22 film.
- Player and team names are caption spellings and may be wrong throughout.

## Q&A

- Outreach: Teamworks already works with every FBS school and most FCS, and high school data is not yet available because quality all-22 video is missing [22:26], [22:58].
- Most advanced college sport: likely baseball and basketball, following professional sport; the speaker expects the gap to close quickly [23:30].

=== FILE: videos/2025-03-18_v-BOAaqS01c_ncaa-2-0-what-s-next/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: v-BOAaqS01c
title: "SSAC25: NCAA 2.0: What's Next?"
event: SSAC25 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Oliver Luck, Mark Jackson (Northwestern athletic director), Brian Higgins (NCAA), moderator Michael mccan (caption spelling, University of New Hampshire School of Law); introduced by Ryan smard (caption spelling)]
topics: [policy, american-football]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A panel discusses what the pending House settlement would change in college sports: direct payments and revenue sharing, a fair-market-value clearinghouse for NIL deals, and what it leaves unresolved (employee status, transfers, eligibility). Panelists cover how money might be divided between football and other sports, private equity, conference realignment, the transfer portal and a ten-year outlook. Views are opinion and prediction from an athletic director, a former NCAA executive and an NCAA business executive. The panel is set before a court hearing on the settlement, so nothing here confirms what was approved. There is no analytics content in the sense of data or models.

## Key claims

- The settlement has two parts: back payments of about $2.8 billion over ten years for past lost NIL and broadcast revenue, and revenue sharing of up to 22% of certain revenues among opting-in schools [01:02], [01:33], [02:03].
- The moderator argues the true share is closer to 50% once scholarships and other benefits are counted [02:03].
- Objections include Title IX (most money going to men's sports, especially football) and conflicts with state NIL laws [02:33].
- NIL deals above $600 would go through a clearinghouse for a fair-market-value check [03:03].
- The settlement leaves open whether athletes are employees, transfer rules, and eligibility [03:34], [04:04], [04:36].
- Jackson says he now feels like a CEO focused on revenue, and that Northwestern has one of the smallest alumni and ticket bases in the Big 10 [06:09], [06:39].
- Luck expects a light regulatory touch on fair-market value at first, and says disclosure rules of the past three years were ignored with no penalties as far as he can tell [08:12], [08:43], [09:13].
- Higgins says a new entity separate from the NCAA will manage the cap and disclosure, so the national office will spend more on data and marketing to help schools raise revenue [09:44], [10:16], [10:46].
- Luck says a paid player does not disrupt a locker room if the right players are paid [11:47].
- Jackson says large media-rights deals might be restructured so some of the money flows as NIL through the clearinghouse, pushing a school's total above the cap; Northwestern cannot do this [12:48].
- Higgins says the national office wants fair pay for athletes while keeping the field level enough that small programs can still win titles [13:48], [14:18].
- Higgins expects more scholarships post-settlement, with disproportionate growth for women's sports, and cites a new performance fund in the women's basketball championship [16:52], [17:23].
- Luck says schools are using the judge's backward-looking formula as a safe harbor, a split of 75% football, 15% men's basketball, 5% women's basketball, 5% others [19:24].
- Luck doubts private equity has a role, since the SEC and Big 10 say they can fund themselves; Jackson has been pitched and calls it expensive money; Higgins says any capital must earn more than its cost [21:56], [22:27], [22:59], [24:01].
- Luck describes the ACC arrangement sending 60% of a pool to schools with the best TV ratings, and thinks the settlement could bring five to seven stable years [25:02], [25:34].
- On the transfer portal, Luck says individual contracts (no-transfer periods, clawbacks) will matter most, and a league-wide transfer limit would be a likely antitrust problem [31:44], [32:14], [32:46].
- Higgins says many transfers are healthy and transfer rates in other sports are not much different from the general student body [30:42], [31:13].
- Luck predicts athletes in revenue sports will be found to be employees, unionize and bargain collectively, which he thinks would improve college athletics [34:47], [35:17], [35:48].
- Jackson compares today to the AFL-NFL era and expects free agency, bargaining and a cap to evolve; he hopes Congress builds a framework protecting Olympic sports [36:49], [37:19].
- Higgins wants all sports treated as commercial products, to avoid cutting sports, and to keep graduation rates [37:51], [38:22].

## Numbers and definitions

- Hearing date April 7 [01:02].
- $2.8 billion over ten years, to athletes going back to about 2017 [01:02], [01:33].
- Revenue sharing up to 22% [01:33]; direct-payment cap initially about $21 million [02:03]; Jackson calls it $20 and a half million [12:18]. A later "up to 205 million" [15:20] is likely a caption error.
- Clearinghouse threshold $600 [03:03]; a later "$61" deal [09:13] is a caption problem.
- Northwestern: hundred-million organization [06:09]; $850 million stadium [18:24]; 21 sports [18:54].
- Baseball scholarship limit 11.3 going to 35 [16:52], [43:33].
- Split 75, 15, 5, 5 [19:24].
- ACC: 60% of a revenue pool to top-rated schools [25:34]. Luck says 17 members "I think" [25:34].
- Settlement is a ten-year deal; some TV contracts up in 30, 31 and 32 [25:02].
- NCAA has 91 championships, hoping for 95 [10:46], [38:22].
- Swim trials drew 35,000 versus 1500 at the NCAA championship [39:23].
- Division 2 and 3 get "4 point something" and "3 point something" percent of national office revenue (as captioned) [43:33].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Fair-market-value review of NIL deals by a new entity, with Luck suggesting Deloitte builds a complex algorithm [08:12]. The moderator-cited details are not shown.
- Backward-looking allocation formula from the judge [19:24].
- Collective bargaining and the non-statutory labor exemption as a route around antitrust limits [35:17].

## Limits and open questions

- Everything is opinion or forecast; no data or analysis is shown.
- The settlement outcome is not in the talk; the hearing is still ahead.
- The moderator states that a Department of Education fact sheet on equal distribution was withdrawn [19:54].
- Panelists represent interested institutions (an athletic director, a former NCAA executive now consulting, an NCAA executive); Jackson says his general counsel told him to give no numbers [17:53].
- The 75, 15, 5, 5 split and the ACC 60% figure are Luck's secondhand descriptions.
- Names (Wilkin, Petitti, Deloitte, Kellogg) are as captioned and may be wrong.

## Q&A

- Olympic sports: Higgins says the NCAA, national governing bodies and the Olympic committee must work together, and notes the US lacks public funding for elite athletes [38:52], [39:23], [39:54].
- International athletes and NIL: visa law was not built for NIL and likely needs federal change; workarounds exist [40:25], [40:56], [41:27].
- Balancing athletes and Big 10 interests: Jackson says there is alignment so far [41:27], [41:59].
- Division 2 and 3: Higgins thinks they benefit as roster caps push players down, and notes a dedicated share of national office revenue [43:02], [43:33], [44:03].
- Should football have different rules: Luck hopes not, but says it already differs and the rest of the system would adapt [44:34], [45:04].

=== FILE: videos/2026-04-09_6QCe9Gndj44_from-tool-sprawl-to-competitive-advantage-rebuilding-coheren/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: 6QCe9Gndj44
title: "SSAC26: From Tool Sprawl to Competitive Advantage: Rebuilding Coherent Analytics"
event: SSAC26 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Loram Abdallah (caption spelling), Data Bricks practice director at Luminata (caption spelling); Shue Yang (caption spelling), senior solution architect at Data Bricks; introduced by Judy Sherman]
topics: [front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Two speakers, one from a consultancy and one from Databricks, argue that media companies and professional franchises have a coherence problem, not a data problem: metrics are defined in different places and staff spend time asking which number is right. They describe modernizing a live campaign platform for a large media organization by centralizing business definitions and governance on a lakehouse with Unity Catalog, then extend the idea to player performance, fan and sponsorship data. The talk is a vendor and consultant pitch. It shows a reference architecture and qualitative outcomes, and no measured results. There is little sport-specific content.

## Key claims

- Most media companies and franchises have a coherence problem; alignment, not data volume, decides whether analytics creates advantage [01:00], [01:32].
- In their scenario, three days of different numbers for the same campaign shift the conversation from optimizing to reconciling [02:35], [03:07].
- They say franchises have the same pattern: coaching, scouting and commercial staff using different metrics for similar things [03:07].
- When alignment breaks, decisions slow; the speaker says the cause is architecture, not talent [03:40], [04:14].
- In the case described, audience data sat in several systems, scripts did publishing and another team owned orchestration [04:45].
- The turning point was to stop asking which tools to add and instead centralize business logic and shared semantics [06:49], [07:21], [07:55].
- The Databricks speaker says traditional catalogs cover only tables, auditing and access, while Unity Catalog governs models, agents and endpoints and can federate outside sources without copies [08:56], [09:28], [09:59], [10:30].
- Business semantics defined once in Unity Catalog can serve reports and give AI agents context; the speaker says external BI tools each use their own semantic layers with less metadata [11:33], [14:07], [14:38].
- The implementation used Delta Lake for storage, Unity Catalog for governance, Lakeflow jobs for orchestration and Databricks SQL, with campaign and audience definitions moved into governed tables [16:13], [16:45], [17:16].
- Lakebase was not implemented in this project; the speaker says the architecture now supports operational workloads without a new silo [17:16].
- Outcomes named are structural: less pipeline upkeep, clearer ownership, better cost visibility, stable definitions, and more trust [17:16], [17:47].
- Stated business effects: faster optimization cycles, consistent audience definitions, trust in metrics, and scalable governance [18:18], [18:48], [19:18], [19:50].
- The same pattern is said to apply to player performance analytics, fan engagement, ticketing and sponsorship reporting [19:50], [20:22].
- Shared semantics are described as a basis for AI readiness [20:54], [21:25].

## Numbers and definitions

- Talk: 20 minutes plus 5 minutes of Q&A [00:30].
- Delivery estimate: 3 to 4 months, depending on company size and scope [24:30].
- One engineer architecting with four or five parallel agents writing code [23:59].
- "Business semantics": definitions of metrics and entities (audiences, yield) defined once and reused [07:21], [11:33].
- Medallion gold layer: data ready for downstream use [12:36]. No quantitative performance numbers are given.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Reference architecture: siloed data moved to cloud object storage, refined through layers to a gold layer, with governance and a semantic layer over it [12:04], [12:36], [15:10].
- Delta Lake, Unity Catalog, Lakeflow jobs, Databricks SQL, Lakebase (proposed next step) [13:06], [16:13], [17:16].
- Metric views as the semantic layer feeding agents [14:38].

## Limits and open questions

- No metrics of success (time saved, cost, error rates) are shown.
- Commercial source: a Databricks employee and a consultancy describe products and services they sell.
- The case is one media organization; sports examples are speculative ("can appear") [19:50].
- The speed claim rests on engineers working with parallel AI agents and is stated as the speaker's estimate [23:59], [24:30].
- Caption problems: the firm is spelled "Luminata" and "Lumin Alta," the lead speaker is addressed as "Jerome," and Lakebase appears as "Lake Base."

## Q&A

- How long does the process take: the speaker estimates 3 to 4 months, done with engineers directing parallel AI agents [23:29], [23:59], [24:30].

=== FILE: videos/2026-04-09_8qKJw2Dh7dk_setting-the-edge-how-analytics-are-rewriting-football-strate/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: 8qKJw2Dh7dk
title: "SSAC26: Setting the Edge: How Analytics are Rewriting Football Strategy"
event: SSAC26 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Karim Kassam (caption spelling "Kassam"), Teamworks; Nick Caserio, Houston Texans; Connor Barwin, Philadelphia Eagles; moderator Mina Kimes, ESPN; introduced by Quinn McCarthy]
topics: [american-football, front-office, decision-making]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Three football executives and a moderator discuss how data has changed player evaluation, development and in-game decisions. Barwin recalls early performance tracking as high friction, Caserio stresses integration across departments and simple, position-specific measures, and Kassam describes tracking-derived metrics and AI models. On fourth downs, the panel says analytics points toward aggression on average but the head coach decides with game context. The panel also covers communication to coaches, players and fans, and how to handle small samples. Much of it is anecdote and opinion from people whose organizations sell or use these tools.

## Key claims

- Barwin says he had little awareness of advanced stats when he entered the league in 2009, and that the 2013 Eagles were at the forefront of performance tracking [01:33], [02:03].
- Barwin says daily HRV, hydration and survey checks created too much friction then, and that things are much better now [03:34].
- Caserio says data was once viewed as something that could be used against players; it is now more conversational and players want their measurements [04:35], [05:05].
- Caserio says more teams now build a performance area with resources and staff [05:36].
- Kassam describes data eras: box score data, play-by-play, then tracking data at 10 times a second, and says this allows measures such as change of direction and how a player affects the pocket or run game [06:36], [07:06], [07:36], [08:06].
- Kassam's get-off metric for edge rushers has a flat age curve in his analysis, which he reads as meaning players can improve it; deep speed might fall off faster [08:06], [08:36], [10:10].
- Computer vision now lets similar data be derived from all-22 film for college players [10:10].
- Barwin says at least 25 players each week get no game data, which is a chance to use data for development [11:41].
- Caserio says data use only works if analytics, coaches and scouting are integrated and communicate constantly [12:43].
- Caserio says coaches want digestible information with an application, and that one must be flexible between old and new school [13:44], [14:15].
- Caserio says the 2026 combine 40 times were fast as a group because of specific training, that about three-quarters of the drills are not real-world applicable, and that time speed and game speed can differ [15:47], [16:17].
- Barwin says combine numbers matter as an important part of a bigger puzzle [17:49].
- Kassam says football differs from baseball because roles and schemes differ, and that his metrics adjust for conference and level of competition [18:50], [19:20].
- Kassam says his pass rush metric treats the pocket as a surface to isolate one player's effect, and that such measures can be stable from college to pro [19:51], [20:21].
- Caserio says to keep measures simple and tied to what the position requires [20:52], [21:22].
- On fourth downs, Caserio says the philosophy is set before the game and the head coach decides [22:23], [22:54]; Barwin says decisions are prepared during the week, then injuries, weather and feel for the game matter [24:26], [24:56].
- Barwin says explaining the why to players builds confidence [25:26].
- Kassam says his own models showed teams should be more aggressive on average but with large error bars and many gray-zone cases [27:27], [27:57].
- Caserio says the plus-35 to 40 area is the hardest, and field position and the team's defense enter the calculus [28:28], [28:59].
- Kassam says a run-game neural network trained on a couple million plays credits hustle and penalizes loafing without being told [31:31], [32:01], [32:32].
- Caserio says AI is here and staff should experiment with use cases; his performance team uses a model to synthesize articles [33:33], [34:03].
- Kassam says tracking-based trait language (change of direction, accuracy) helps scouts, coaches and analysts speak the same language [34:33], [35:03].
- Barwin says big plays often happen because someone did not do what they were supposed to, which models would find hard to learn [35:33], [36:03].
- Barwin says analytics and coaches both overload people; show the few items you have conviction on, and say so when it is an experiment [39:06], [39:38], [40:08].

## Numbers and definitions

- Barwin entered the league in 2009 [01:33]; Eagles change in 2013 [02:03].
- Box score era around 2009; play-by-play by 2013 with about 100 times more data; Next Gen Stats in 2019; locations 10 times a second [07:06], [07:36]. Another talk in this batch gives 2018 and "a thousand times" for similar steps.
- Danielle Hunter (caption spelling), age 31 [09:39].
- At least 25 players not playing each week [11:41].
- Three-quarters of combine drills not applicable [15:47]; corner ran 4.65 (captions give a garbled name) [16:17].
- Plus-35 to 40 gray zone; scoring probability from minus 10 to minus 15 versus minus 40 [28:28], [28:59].
- Head coach has about two or three seconds to decide (speaker unclear in captions) [27:57].
- Run-game model trained on a couple million running plays [31:31]; Gibbs 18 yards [32:32]. Another talk in this batch gives about 100,000 plays.
- Caserio: four-week blocks, about eight to 10 games before teams are well known, 17 games [40:08], [40:39].
- Kassam: about 60 pass rush snaps for a get-off estimate, about 200 routes for receiver COD [41:09], [41:41].
- Roster: 20 offense, 22 defense and three specialists, as captioned (likely garbled) [44:45].
- Super Bowl team with three active receivers [44:45].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Get-off metric from tracking data and film [08:06], [08:36].
- Pass rush model treating the pocket as a surface [19:51].
- Run-game neural network attributing credit among 22 players [31:31].
- Projection system combining a player's history with current small samples [41:41].
- Four-week review blocks for team performance [40:39].
- Practice tracking over several years to benchmark players [43:14].
- Pre-game philosophy and a game management coordinator for fourth downs [22:23].

## Limits and open questions

- Mostly anecdote; no data or results are shown on get-off aging, practice tracking or fourth-down outcomes.
- Kassam is a vendor executive describing his own company's metrics.
- Caption problems: Barwin's answer at [23:56] says "Nick wants to be aggressive" though the panel lists Caserio with the Texans and Barwin with the Eagles; the referent is unclear. Player names (Kemoko Turay, Kamari, Moro, Jobe) are unreliable.
- Kassam says the public and some commentators do not see that models know the roster, including defense [28:59], [29:30].
- The moderator asks about PFF grades; a speaker says most players do not like them, with no detail [37:04].
- Caserio says a limit of AI is that no database captures everything on the field [36:03]. The statement is in the moderator's turn and is unclear.

## Q&A

- Adjusting to small samples: Caserio says break the season into four-week blocks; Kassam says some metrics resolve quickly and uses projection; Barwin says practice tracking history gave confidence in one player [40:39], [41:09], [41:41], [43:14].
- Keeping judgment on a small-sample player: Barwin says know your own players and track practice [42:43], [43:14].
- Game-day roster decisions: Caserio says they depend on how you plan to play and who is available, with an example of three active receivers [44:45].

One line on caption problems and unverifiable claims: video 4 has garbled speaker and player names, an unclear "Nick wants to be aggressive" at [23:56], and a likely garbled roster count at [44:45]; video 2 has caption errors "205 million" [15:20] and "$61" [09:13] and unverifiable figures (75/15/5/5, ACC 60%); video 3 is a vendor pitch with no measured outcomes; across talks 1 and 4 the tracking-data release year (2018 vs 2019), data multiplier and training-play count (about 100,000 vs a couple million) conflict.
